itineraries.title: Guatemala Belize Road Trip 13 days: Maya & Caribbean
itineraries.subtitle: Road trip format, different accommodation almost every night, from Antigua's volcanoes to Caye Caulker's reefs in 13 days.
itineraries.notes: Fast-paced road trip itinerary, 9 different accommodations in 12 days. Combines altitude (1500 m at Antigua, Lake Atitlán) and tropical heat (Petén, Belize coast) with two domestic flights: Guatemala City to Flores, then Dangriga to Belize City or Caye Caulker.
itineraries.climate: Best time: December to April, dry season with 20-28°C in the highlands (Antigua, Atitlán) and 25-32°C on the Caribbean coast. Avoid September-October: daily torrential rains, muddy roads to Tikal, poor jungle visibility. June to November: hurricane risk on Belize's cayes.

visits.text: Let's be honest: Guatemala City won't make you dream, but it's the country's unavoidable gateway. La Aurora Airport drops travelers at 1500 m elevation into a sprawling capital where most visitors spend just one night. If you arrive early, the Popol Vuh Museum in Zona 10 displays one of the country's finest collections of pre-Columbian Maya art. Book your Antigua transfer in advance—the route covers 45 km but takes a solid hour.

activities.text: Take advantage of your arrival to exchange money at the airport (quetzals, decent rate at the official counter) and grab a local SIM card from Tigo or Claro. The terminal ATMs work with international cards. Don't linger downtown after dark—certain neighborhoods have a rough reputation.

practical_info.tip: Book a hotel near Zona 10 or 14, safer and closer to the airport.

visits.text: The scent of roasted coffee hangs over Antigua from dawn, and that's a good thing: the town cultivates some of the country's finest beans on the neighboring slopes. Founded in 1543 as Santiago de los Caballeros, the former capital was partly destroyed by the 1773 earthquake, which paradoxically froze its baroque ruins in time. Stroll from Plaza Mayor in the morning before the sun blazes on the cobblestones.

Founded in 1543, Antigua lost its capital status after the 1773 earthquake—residents fled to present-day Guatemala City. The Palace of the Captains General and the ruins of Santo Domingo Convent bear witness to what it once was. The convent now houses a museum and a five-star hotel; paid access to the historic section but worth every quetzal.

The Santa Catalina Arch is Antigua's obligatory postcard shot—a bright yellow baroque passage with Agua volcano as backdrop. Go before 8am for the crowd-free photo, or late afternoon for golden light. The street leading to the arch, Calle del Arco, is also the town's most photogenic.

The Capuchin Convent deserves a detour for its circular cloister, unique in Guatemala, built in 1736. Admission is modest, around 40 quetzals. The petal-shaped monastic cells and the torre del retiro offer a shortcut to understanding cloistered life in colonial times.

If you climb Cerro de la Cruz at sunrise, you'll embrace all of Antigua—its red rooftops and Agua volcano towering at 3760 meters. The paved trail takes 15 to 20 minutes from the center. Go accompanied—incidents have been reported on the dawn climb; the tourist police sometimes offer free escorts.

activities.text: Guatemalans call Pacaya “the easy volcano”, but easy is relative: 2552 meters, two hours of climbing over solidified lava flows. It is one of the most active volcanoes in the country, and you will see fumaroles and recent lava flows. For the longer experience, Acatenango (3976 m) takes two days, with a high-altitude camp and views of the eruptions of neighboring Fuego. Both volcanoes are reached by shuttle from Antigua: allow a day trip there and back for Pacaya.

practical_info.tip: Pacaya trek: leave in the morning, count on 350 quetzals with guide and transport from Antigua.

activities.text: Take a cooking class to learn pepián, the spiced stew considered the national dish. Several workshops also teach tamales and rellenitos made from plantain. La Tortilla cooking school is well-regarded and fits into two to three hours.

practical_info.tip: Count on about 60 dollars per person, meal included.

activities.text: Roasted beans crack under your fingers at Finca Filadelphia, a plantation accessible in fifteen minutes from downtown. The tour explains everything from planting to cupping. Café Azotea also offers a free coffee museum in an old hacienda.

practical_info.tip: French-language tours available by reservation at Filadelphia.

visits.text: Touristy, yes, but Panajachel remains the best entry point to Lake Atitlán, and all shuttles from Antigua arrive here. The town serves as a logistics hub: agencies, restaurants, boat dock for lanchas to other villages. Book everything upon arrival—boats leave when they're full.

Calle Santander pulses from morning to night—it's Pana's tourist backbone. Huipil textile shops, craft vendors, bohemian cafés, the works. Bargain without guilt—it's the local sport—but know that fifty quetzals make a real difference for vendors.

Formed 84,000 years ago, Lake Atitlán is a caldera ringed by San Pedro, Tolimán, and Atitlán volcanoes. It's Central America's deepest lake, and Aldous Huxley wrote in 1934's Beyond the Mexique Bay that it surpassed Lake Como in beauty. Swimming is possible, but avoid areas near large villages due to periodic cyanobacteria.

activities.text: Climb to Mirador de Panajachel or Cerro de la Cruz for panoramic views of all three volcanoes, especially late afternoon when light turns the lake purple. The trail is short but steep—thirty minutes uphill.

The fresh morning air smells like rain even in dry season: Atitlán Nature Reserve, ten minutes from downtown, offers suspension bridges, a butterfly greenhouse, and cloud forest trails. Count on three hours for the full loop.

practical_info.tip: Admission about 100 quetzals, open 8am to 4pm.

map_keywords: San Juan La Laguna Lake Atitlan

visits.text: San Juan La Laguna's Tz'utujil weaving cooperatives are run by women who still use natural dyes: indigo, cochineal, tree bark. The workshops explain the entire process, from thread to finished huipil. The demonstration takes an hour and directly supports the community.

San Juan La Laguna's alleys explode with murals—works by local naïve painters who exhibit on the street itself. It's the lake's most artistic village, peaceful, without Pana's chaos or San Pedro's backpacker vibe. An hour's stroll covers the whole place.

activities.text: Visit the medicinal plant garden run by a local cooperative that makes soaps, shampoos, and candles from garden plants. You can combine it with a crafting workshop. Free admission, donations appreciated.

Coffee cultivated on San Pedro volcano's slopes is a source of Tz'utujil pride. Several fincas offer the complete tour, from bean to cup, with tasting. Count on two hours and 100 to 150 quetzals depending on the finca.

practical_info.tip: Cooperative La Voz offers tours in Spanish and English.

visits.text: Santiago Atitlán residents move Maximón every year—this syncretic Maya deity, a dressed and hatted wooden statue, changes houses each May. Faithful ensure he always has a lit cigarette in his mouth and a full glass of alcohol. Ask your lancha captain or a tuk-tuk driver where he's staying this year—they know. Bring a few quetzals as an offering.

The Santiago Apóstol church bears the marks of heavy events: the 1981 assassination of priest Stanley Rother and the massacre of fourteen villagers during the civil war. A plaque in the church commemorates these moments. It's also the lake's largest village and the Tz'utujil stronghold least oriented toward tourism.

activities.text: Climb to Mirador del Valle above Santiago to see the entire lake open up and glimpse where it ends—a view impossible from other villages. Fifteen to twenty minutes on foot from downtown. The local market near the dock is worth a detour for its typical embroidery worn by women.

visits.text: Go to Chichicastenango on Sunday, not Thursday—the market is even denser, and vendors come from across the Altiplano. It's one of Central America's largest indigenous markets, though don't claim it's the oldest or largest without nuance: local sources make it a point of national pride—that's enough. Guard your bag and bargain with a cool head.

Built in 1540, Santo Tomás church rises on the foundations of an ancient Maya temple. The eighteen steps leading to its entrance are still considered sacred by the K'iche', and shamans burn incense and copal there daily. This is where the Popol Vuh manuscript, sacred Maya book, was rediscovered in the 18th century. Don't photograph inside, and cover shoulders and knees.

Chichicastenango's cemetery explodes with color: tombstones painted yellow, turquoise, magenta, Maya and Catholic rituals intertwined. Five minutes on foot from the market, the visit is discreet and respectful, especially on days of family offerings.

activities.text: Climb Santo Tomás's steps to see the market from above—the labyrinthine sprawl of stalls becomes legible from up here. The Calvario chapel on the opposite side of the plaza offers the same kind of viewpoint but with fewer crowds.

If you really want to bargain, divide the announced price by two and work your way up slowly. Embroidered huipiles and traditional dance masks are the most typical purchases. Avoid religious feast days like December 7 (Quema del Diablo), when the town closes for business.

visits.text: Flores's pink, yellow, and blue houses reflect in Lake Petén Itzá—the island barely covers 13 hectares and can be crossed on foot in twenty minutes. Connected to the mainland by a causeway, it serves as base for Tikal and Yaxha. The atmosphere shifts quickly: Caribbean, slow, hot.

Before becoming Flores, the island was called Noj Petén, capital of the last independent Maya kingdom—the Itzá resisted the Spanish until 1697, more than 200 years after Columbus's arrival. The conquistadors razed the city, and the modern town rebuilt on its ruins in the 18th century.

The Iglesia Nuestra Señora de los Remedios crowns the island's high point at 127 meters elevation. The colonial church was built with stones from a dismantled Maya pyramid. Climb up for panoramic views of the lake and Petén hills at sunset.

activities.text: Cross by lancha to San Miguel on the north shore (10 quetzals), then climb to Mirador del Rey Canek—fifteen minutes' walk. The wooden platform offers the best photo of the island. Bring repellent—mosquitoes are plentiful.

Sunset from a Flores rooftop is an institution. Several bars and hotels around the island's perimeter have west-facing terraces. A Guatemalan Gallo beer, the lake's shifting colors—it's the relaxation moment before Tikal's big day.

visits.text: Temple IV rises 65 meters, Tikal's tallest pyramid (La Danta at El Mirador, even taller, demands five days of jungle trekking to reach). Built around 741 under the reign of Yik'in Chan K'awiil, it marked the western boundary of the ceremonial center. The wooden staircase leads to the summit where the canopy opens endlessly, pierced by other temple peaks. Sunrise bookings possible, 5:30am on site, sometimes foggy conditions.

Howler monkeys wake Tikal's jungle before dawn—their deep roar carries for several kilometers. The national park covers 576 km² and shelters jaguars, coatis, toucans, over 400 bird species. You'll walk fifteen kilometers in the day—bring water and closed-toe shoes.

Tikal's Gran Plaza aligns two pyramids face to face: Temple I (45 meters, Temple of the Great Jaguar, 682-734) and Temple II (38 meters). The North Acropolis and Central Acropolis border them—you can climb the latter for plunging views. The nobles' residential palace contains about a hundred rooms.

El Mundo Perdido is worth the detour—Tikal's oldest complex, built in the Preclassic era and abandoned around 900 AD. The ceremonial pyramid rises 30 meters—you can climb it for 360° views far less crowded than the Gran Plaza.

Local guides say that George Lucas filmed the rebel base scene on Yavin 4 here for Star Wars Episode IV in 1977. The city peaked between 600 and 800, with up to 60,000 inhabitants in the heart of the urban area.

activities.text: If you can handle a 4am wake-up, the 'sunrise' tour leaves before official opening and places visitors atop Temple IV for sunrise. Mist, howlers, first light on the pyramids—it's the trip's most memorable experience. Count on 250 to 350 quetzals with guide.

practical_info.tip: Park admission 150 quetzals + 100 quetzals for the dawn tour, often cash payment.

activities.text: Spot coatis, keel-billed toucans, and spider monkeys on trails between temple groups. Morning and late afternoon are best. A naturalist guide makes all the difference—otherwise you'll miss half the animals.

visits.text: Yaxha has neither Tikal's size nor its crowds, and that's exactly what makes it worthwhile. One of Petén's major sites, it counts about 500 structures including 9 temple-pyramids, all on the lagoon's edge. Do it before Tikal so you won't be disappointed, or do it for the sunset.

Temple 216 rises 37 meters above the canopy and offers the signature view: Yaxha lagoon, the Topoxté site on its islet, and jungle stretching to the horizon. The wooden staircase replaces the stone stairway that became impassable. Yaxha means 'green water' in Maya, a name unchanged since the Classic era.

Iguanas dart through the stones and howler monkeys settle in trees above the stelae. The minor astronomical complex, erected between 700 and 800 AD, aligns stelae and a four-step pyramid with the solstices. Stela 31 and its carved birds on Plaza F.

activities.text: Stay until sunset atop Temple 216—it's the site's signature experience. Silence is broken only by howlers and toucans returning for the night. Bring water, headlamp for the descent, and strong repellent: mosquitoes emerge at 5pm.

practical_info.tip: Admission 80 quetzals. Site officially closes at 6pm—negotiate with your guide if you want to stay for sunset.

visits.text: The Hawkesworth Bridge, Belize's only suspension bridge, connects San Ignacio to its twin town Santa Elena over the Macal River. It's the classic arrival photo. Main street Burns Avenue concentrates cafés, tour agencies, and the town's lively center.

The Saturday market smells of papaya, habanero pepper, and Marie Sharp's sauce being sampled at stalls. Producers come from across Cayo District: Mennonites, Maya, Creole. This is where you find crafts, fresh fruit, and the trip's best snacks.

The conservation program for endangered green iguanas (hunted for their meat) is worth a stop. At the San Ignacio Resort Hotel, you feed them, hold them and learn about their whole life cycle. 18 Belize dollars, about an hour.

activities.text: Paddle the Macal River by canoe to spot iguanas, herons, and sometimes agoutis. The ride lasts two to three hours from downtown. Barton Creek Cave, an hour's drive away, offers a canoe variant in a Maya underground river.
Belizeans speak of their hot sauce “Marie Sharp” as if it were a religion. The factory makes sixteen different flavors, from mild to “Beware”. Buy it directly at any stall in the market.

If you like thrills, cave tubing at Nohoch Che'en (Caves Branch) means drifting on an inner tube down an underground river lit by headlamp, a 45-minute ride. It can be combined with a zipline over the jungle. The site is reached by car from San Ignacio: allow a day trip there and back.

practical_info.tip: Count on 70 to 90 USD per person for the tubing + zipline combo with transport and lunch.

activities.text: Try rice and beans with stew chicken—Belize's national dish, served everywhere with potato salad and plantain. Ko-Ox Han Nah on Burns Avenue is the safe bet. Also ask for 'one barrel rum,' the best local rum by popular vote.

visits.text: Cahal Pech overlooks San Ignacio from its hilltop—modest-sized but well-preserved Maya ruins: 34 structures, two ball courts, several residential temples. The site was the elite residence of a ruling Maya family occupied from the Preclassic (1200 BC) to Late Classic. Admission costs about 5 US dollars and the visit takes an hour. Small museum at the entrance for context before the walk.

activities.text: Go early morning, 7-8am—you'll have the site almost to yourself, agoutis and toucans are active in the trees. Ten minutes on foot from downtown San Ignacio, steep climb at the end. Good warm-up before the more impressive Xunantunich in the afternoon.

practical_info.tip: Open daily 6am-6pm (April-Oct) or 6:30am-5pm (Oct-April).

visits.text: The hand-crank ferry creaks across the Mopan River, operated by a ferryman who turns the wheel by arm strength—it's the only access to Xunantunich site. The crossing takes one minute, free of charge, tip welcome. Four cars maximum on board. The approach via this artisanal crossing is half the experience.

El Castillo climbs to 40 meters, Belize's second tallest structure after Caracol. Built from 800 AD onward, it bears an elaborate frieze on its east façade depicting the sun god, moon, and Venus—the original is protected by a fiberglass replica. The west frieze was uncovered in 2016.

activities.text: Climb to El Castillo's summit—the interior staircase leads to two vaulted chambers and the top, panoramic views over the Mopan valley into Guatemala (border 1 km west). Go early morning—the site opens at 8am—you'll avoid heat and the 10am tourist peak.

practical_info.tip: Admission 5 USD. Public bus to Benque from San Ignacio, get off at the ferry landing.

visits.text: ATM Cave is Belize's most memorable experience according to nearly every traveler, and National Geographic ranked it #1 worldwide in its top sacred caves. Actun Tunichil Muknal means 'cave of the stone sepulcher' in Maya. Fourteen skeletons rest in the main chamber, including the Crystal Maiden, calcified and sparkling for over a thousand years. No photos allowed inside since 2012.

activities.text: The tour starts with 45 minutes walking through jungle, three river crossings on foot, then a swim to enter the cave through an hourglass mouth partially submerged. Three hours inside between swimming, light climbing, and walking in wet socks (shoes stay at the artifact chamber entrance). Helmet and headlamp provided. Mandatory guide, departure from San Ignacio.

practical_info.tip: 110 to 140 USD per person. Dry season (December-May) recommended—the cave can close during floods.

activities.text: If you're claustrophobic or not very athletic, tell your guide beforehand: some passages are tight and several hours of effort are required. Guides are used to claustrophobes—it usually works out. Avoid with heart or back problems. Not for young children (12 years minimum).

visits.text: The Garifuna of Hopkins come from a singular history: a mix of shipwrecked African slaves and Caribbean Arawaks, exiled by the British in 1797 from Saint Vincent to Honduras, then migrating on to Belize. Language, songs, drumming, hudut: everything is alive, not turned into heritage.

Three kilometers of golden sand and wooden fishing boats—that's Hopkins beachside. No giant resort, small oceanfront hotels, thatched-roof bars, wooden piers reaching into turquoise water. The village was named 'Friendliest Village in Belize' by Belize First magazine, and you feel it.

The Lebeha Drumming Center has trained village children in Garifuna percussion for twenty years. Evening workshops are open to visitors: three or four drums, one voice, sometimes a dancer in a full skirt. Paranda and punta rhythms can be learned in an hour—poorly, but you learn them.

activities.text: Learn hudut during a Garifuna cooking class: fish cooked in coconut milk, plantain pounded in a mortar, spicy cassava root sauce. Several village houses offer the workshop by reservation, meal included, around 50 USD.

If you're there on November 19, you'll catch Garifuna Settlement Day: reenactment of the canoe arrival from Honduras, parades, drums all night. Book accommodation six months in advance—prices double and everything fills up.

Snorkeling at South Water Caye Marine Reserve, about 12 miles offshore, is the big outing from Hopkins. Reef less crowded than Caye Caulker, crystal water, rays and turtles. Count on 120 to 150 USD for the day with lunch on an island. Ask for Happy Go Luckie Tours.

practical_info.tip: Departure around 8am, return 4pm. Reef-safe sunscreen required.

activities.text: Bike along the village from north (Baila) to south (False Sittee)—three kilometers of sandy track by the sea. Most hotels rent bikes for 5 USD half-day. It's the best way to see how Hopkins really lives, away from the hotel circuit.

visits.text: Cockscomb Basin was created in 1986 as the world's first reserve dedicated to protecting the jaguar, on the initiative of biologist Alan Rabinowitz. The sanctuary covers about 400 km² on the eastern slopes of the Maya Mountains. It is home to jaguars, pumas, ocelots, margays and jaguarundis: the five felines of Belize.

Over 200 jaguars live here, and you probably won't see a single one—they're nocturnal and shy. That's the honest warning to give before visiting. On the other hand, over 290 bird species, howler monkeys, coatis, and sometimes fresh jaguar tracks on muddy trails—that compensates.

activities.text: Walk the Ben's Bluff Trail to the waterfall and its swimmable basin—4 km round trip with 170 meters elevation gain. The Wari Loop, shorter and flat, is ideal for morning birds. Bring closed-toe shoes, water, strong repellent: Cockscomb receives over 100 inches of rain per year—it's one of Belize's wettest corners.

practical_info.tip: Admission 10 BZD for non-nationals. 6 miles of unpaved track from Maya Centre, 4x4 recommended.

activities.text: Tubing on South Stann Creek is worth it after the hike: rent an inner tube at the visitor center for 7.5 USD and float an hour with the current. At the sanctuary's campground or dorms, you can sleep on-site (10 to 80 USD depending on comfort) and attempt a guided night walk to hear jaguars.

visits.text: The Split, a gap created by Hurricane Hattie in 1961, cuts Caye Caulker in two and becomes the island's social hub. Bar, turquoise water, tree jumpers, kayakers—this is where you spend late afternoons. The island's north side, little developed, is reached by ferry from The Split.

Caye Caulker's sand roads are explored on foot or by golf cart; there are no cars on the island. The local motto “Go Slow” is painted everywhere. Three main streets, brightly colored wooden houses, thatched-roof restaurants serving grilled lobster in season (mid-June to mid-February).

Hol Chan, created in 1987, protects 18 km² of coral reef, seagrass beds and mangroves at the southern tip of Ambergris Caye, the neighbouring island, reached by boat from Caye Caulker. It is Belize's oldest marine reserve, part of the second-largest barrier reef in the world. Depth varies from 1.5 m to 9 m, ideal for snorkelling.

The local motto 'Go Slow' isn't a tourist slogan—it's what residents tell everyone, especially speeding golf carts. Caye Caulker has deliberately stayed small, without big hotels, unlike neighboring Ambergris Caye. The unanimous verdict: you plan two days, you stay five.

activities.text: Dive in at Shark Ray Alley to swim with nurse sharks and southern stingrays, calm and used to swimmers. The combined Hol Chan + Shark Ray Alley tour lasts about 5.5 hours, with several stops and lunch included. Allow 70 to 100 USD depending on the operator. Book with Black Hawk or Salt Life.

practical_info.tip: Flotation vest available, accessible to non-swimmers. GoPro photos sometimes included.

activities.text: If you're a certified diver, the Great Blue Hole is reached from Caye Caulker in about 2.5 hours by boat. Three dives in the day, including the descent to 40 meters in the sinkhole formed 10,000 years ago. Count on 280 to 350 USD, full day, 6am-5pm.

practical_info.tip: Advanced Open Water certification required. Book 48 hours in advance.

activities.text: Sunset at the Split is an institution. Lazy Lizard serves neon rum punch. For some calm, head to the west shore of the island, far less busy.

visits.text: Belize City has little to hold travelers—it's essentially the transit hub to Philip Goldson International Airport. The city suffered from repeated hurricanes (1931, Hattie in 1961) and the capital was moved to Belmopan in 1970. A few hours suffice before catching your return flight or the water taxi to reach the islands.

activities.text: Make a stop at the Museum of Belize, installed in a former colonial red-brick prison. Small well-organized collection: Maya artifacts, British colonial history, local fauna, old bills and stamps. An hour suffices. Admission about 10 USD for foreigners.

practical_info.tip: Open Monday to Friday 8am-5pm, Saturday 8am-12pm. Closed Sunday.

seo.h1_title: Guatemala Belize Road Trip 13 days: Maya & Caribbean
seo.intro_paragraph: This 13 days Guatemala-Belize combination crosses two registers: the Maya highlands around Antigua, Lake Atitlán, and Tikal, then Belize's Caribbean coast with its caves, Garifuna villages, and barrier reef. The route follows the classic path for travelers who don't want to choose between pre-Columbian culture and the reef.
seo.seo_hook: Colonial Antigua, Lake Atitlán, Chichicastenango market, Tikal pyramids, ATM cave, and Caye Caulker snorkeling in 13 days.
featured_list: Antigua: UNESCO-listed baroque former capital at the foot of three volcanoes
Lake Atitlán: volcanic caldera and Tz'utujil villages accessible by lancha
Chichicastenango: Central America's largest Maya market on Thursdays and Sundays
Tikal: Temple IV at 65 meters, the site's tallest pyramid, above the Petén canopy
Actun Tunichil Muknal: sacred Maya cave with the calcified Crystal Maiden
Caye Caulker: Hol Chan reef, nurse sharks, and sunset at The Split

itineraries.title: Guatemala & Belize in 13 Days: Mayas and the Caribbean
itineraries.subtitle: You'll settle in for 2 nights at each base, from Antigua to Caye Caulker, weaving between Mayan cities and Caribbean beaches.
itineraries.notes: Resort-style format: 5 extended bases (Antigua 2 nights, Flores 2, San Ignacio 2, Hopkins 2, Caye Caulker 2), with day trips from each base. Possible extensions if you have 2–3 extra days: Yaxhá and sunset over the lagoon from Flores, Cockscomb Basin jaguar reserve from Hopkins. Cross-border itinerary—plan for the border formality at Melchor de Mencos. Domestic flight recommended between Guatemala City and Flores to save two days of driving.
itineraries.climate: Best period: November to April (dry season), with 15–25°C in the highlands and 25–30°C in the jungle and Caribbean coast. Avoid May–October: daily rains in the Petén and hurricane risk in Belize (June–November). Humidity is high year-round in the lowlands.

visits.text: La Aurora Airport greets you in Guatemala City, and that's about all you need from it. The capital lacks the colonial charm of Antigua, and security concerns make wandering ill-advised. Grab your rental car or shuttle and head to Antigua, 45 minutes away. If your flight arrives late, sleep near the airport rather than downtown—easier the next morning.

activities.text: Dive into the pedestrianized 6th Avenue in Zona 1—this is where Guatemala City reveals itself best: street vendors, street markets, locals heading home from work. Mercado Central, just behind the cathedral, is ideal for tasting your first local meal (chicken pepián, tamales) and observing daily life without a tourist filter.

In the evening, head to Zona 10 for a drink on a terrace. This upscale district is a complete contrast to the historic center—skyscrapers, contemporary art galleries, restaurants. It's the right place to catch your breath before the three weeks ahead.
Prepare your gear for the eastern part of the country—bring cash, as ATMs become scarce from Río Dulce onward. Dine in the Zona Viva for one last urban evening before several days in nature.

Evening in the Zona Viva (Zona 10): this is the capital's liveliest neighborhood, with a concentration of restaurants and cafés open late. After three weeks in villages and jungle, it's a pleasant transition before departure.

Transfer to La Aurora International Airport (GUA), located in Zona 13, 15 to 30 minutes from Zona Viva depending on traffic. Guatemala City traffic can be very heavy during rush hours—allow plenty of time, at least 2 hours before your flight.

visits.text: Touristy without being overrun, Antigua delivers on its promise. Founded in 1543, the former capital of the Kingdom of Guatemala was destroyed by the 1773 earthquake then abandoned, which paradoxically saved its grid layout and baroque monuments. UNESCO-listed in 1979. Two days suffice for the center; add a day if you want to climb a volcano.

The neon-yellow Santa Catalina Arch frames Volcán de Agua on clear days—it's the cliché photo of Antigua. Built in the 17th century to connect the convent to the school without the nuns being seen, the arch gets mobbed by 9 a.m. Come before 7:30 a.m. for the light and the absence of vendors.

Destroyed by the 1773 earthquake, the Cathedral of Santiago de Antigua was never rebuilt. The small current church occupies the former entrance hall, and the open-air ruins with columns, arches, and plant-invaded altars are well worth the visit. Paid entry to the ruins at the back, about 30 quetzales.

A ruin and yet a living place: Las Capuchinas. This 18th-century convent preserves a unique rotunda with eighteen nuns' cells arranged in a star around a circular patio. The play of light in mid-morning is superb. Less crowded than the cathedral.

Guatemalans call Hermano Pedro their first saint, canonized in 2002. His tomb is in the Church of San Francisco, where hundreds of pilgrims come to pray every day. Buy a candle at the entrance, light it—you'll do what everyone does. Impressive multi-domed architecture from the forecourt.

activities.text: Climb Cerro de la Cruz early in the morning for the view over Antigua and Volcán de Agua in the background. Twenty minutes' walk from the center, free, tourist police presence on the trail. At 6:30 a.m. you'll have it to yourself. Avoid it in the evening and alone, though.

practical_info.tip: Trail monitored until sunset, but mornings are better for light and coolness.

activities.text: The smell of roasted cacao wafts from several chocolate workshops in the center. ChocoMuseo offers two-hour sessions where you grind your beans on a stone metate, from fruit to bar. Free museum entry, workshops about $25. The Maya used cacao as currency.

practical_info.tip: Book the workshop the day before, especially in high season December–March.

activities.text: Book the Acatenango hike the day before if you want to see Fuego spewing live. Two days, one night camping at 3,700 meters, departure around 8 a.m. Difficult (1,500 m elevation gain), warm gear provided by serious agencies. The nighttime spectacle of the neighboring volcano justifies the effort.

practical_info.tip: Choose an agency with quality equipment (Wicho & Charlie's, OX Expeditions), not the cheapest.

visits.text: San Juan La Laguna is worth it, San Pedro is not. Lake Atitlán, a caldera formed 84,000 years ago and surrounded by three volcanoes (San Pedro, Tolimán, Atitlán), shelters eleven villages with very different personalities. San Juan: street art, Tz'utujil textile cooperatives, coffee. Santiago: traditional market, veneration of Maximón. San Pedro: backpackers in binge-drinking mode.

activities.text: Take the lancha early in the morning from Panajachel—the lake is mirror-smooth and the light beats any filter. About 25 quetzales per trip to San Juan or Santiago; ask for the last return time before you leave. Three villages in a day is doable. Four and you'll miss your siesta.

practical_info.tip: Shared public lancha—wait until it's full or pay the difference.

visits.text: Incense, copal, and blue smoke saturate the steps of Santo Tomás Church in Chichicastenango. Built in 1540 on a pre-Columbian Mayan platform, the church is still an active ceremonial center where K'iche' priests and Catholics coexist. The eighteen steps are said to represent the months of the Mayan calendar. Climb to the top to see the market from above.

The colorful cemetery behind the church blends tombs painted blue, pink, green with Mayan-Catholic rituals. Free stroll, quiet in early morning, popular with photographers in late afternoon. Stay discreet: these are active burial sites, not a backdrop.

activities.text: If you come on a Thursday or Sunday, Central America's largest market spreads across hundreds of stalls: embroidered huipils, dance masks, pottery, copal, medicinal plants. On other days, the town is calm and more authentic. Bargain firmly but respectfully—it's expected.

practical_info.tip: Arrive before 8 a.m. to see the stalls being set up and the morning ceremonies.

visits.text: The last Mayan capital to fall to the Spanish, in 1697—two centuries after the collapse of the highlands. Flores sits on a small 2.5 km² island in Lake Petén Itzá, connected to the mainland by a causeway. The high point, where the great Itzá temple once stood, is now occupied by the white cathedral. Plan two nights for Tikal and wandering the island.

Pastel facades, red roofs, and turquoise lake make Flores one of Guatemala's most beautiful small towns, alongside Antigua. Walking around the island takes an hour, best at 6 p.m. for the light. Rooftop terraces on the west side for sunset, waterside terraces on the south side for cocktails.

The Cathedral of Our Lady of Remedies occupies the summit of the island, exactly where the great Itzá temple destroyed in 1697 once stood. The colonial building itself is unremarkable, but the forecourt offers 360° views over the lake. Mayan sculptures from the Ixlú site scattered around the central kiosk.

activities.text: Rent a kayak or lancha at sunset to reach the Mirador de Canek on the north shore. Twenty minutes by boat, short walk, tree hut with panoramic view. Taco and empanada stands set up in the evening at the causeway entrance, about 5 quetzales per piece.

practical_info.tip: Negotiate the lake tour at local price, about 200 quetzales for two hours.

activities.text: Eat along the causeway in the evening: empanadas, tacos, Guatemalan burritos for a few quetzales. Restaurant-wise on the island, La Casa de Enrico (chef in the kitchen) and Raíces del Lago (lake whitefish) stand out. San Telmo: bohemian vibe, lake view, reasonable prices.

practical_info.tip: Prices double on the island compared to the rest of Guatemala—the price of tourism.

visits.text: The howl of howler monkeys precedes the appearance of the pyramids. Tikal National Park spans 576 km² of jungle, UNESCO-listed in 1979 on dual natural and cultural criteria—one of the few in the world. The city prospered from the 4th century BC to the 10th century AD, with around 60,000 inhabitants at its peak circa 700 AD.

Temple IV reaches 70 meters, among the tallest Mayan pyramids accessible to visitors. Built around 741 AD, its summit emerges from the canopy and served as a backdrop in Star Wars Episode IV for the Rebel base on Yavin. Wooden staircase on the side for the climb, spectacular view at sunrise or sunset. Temple I on the Gran Plaza is no longer climbable after falls.

activities.text: If you pay the sunrise supplement (100 quetzales extra), entry at 4 a.m. and access to Temple IV above the canopy. Mist, monkey cries, gradual light: worth the short night. If the sky is cloudy (frequent in wet season), it's less interesting than sunset.

practical_info.tip: Park entry 150 quetzales, tickets only on-site at the booth 20 minutes from the site.

visits.text: San Ignacio's Saturday market smells of ripe papaya, pollo asado, and pupusa browning. On the banks of the Macal River, this Mayan, Kriol, Mennonite, and Garifuna melting pot is the economic hub of the entire Cayo. Pupusas for a US dollar, tacos, medicinal herbs, crafts. Go in the morning for the bustle.

The Hawkesworth Suspension Bridge, the only one of its kind in Belize, links San Ignacio to its twin town Santa Elena across the Macal River. Built in 1949, still in service. Burns Avenue concentrates cafés, bars, and tour agencies, relaxed backpacker vibe. Good base for two nights with day trips.

activities.text: Book a chocolate workshop at AJAW Chocolate right in the center. Twenty US dollars per person, sessions every hour from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday. You grind your beans on a volcanic stone mill, add chili or honey to your taste. Free fresh cacao drink included. The Maya invented chocolate.

practical_info.tip: No reservation needed, walk-ins possible, but arrive early in high season.

activities.text: Mountain Pine Ridge deserves a full day: pine forest at 1,000 meters above sea level, Rio Frio Cave, Rio On Pools (swimming on granite slabs), Big Rock Falls. Allow a day trip there and back from San Ignacio. An operator-run tour is recommended, the road is a dirt track, 4x4 essential.

practical_info.tip: Swimsuit, hiking shoes, mosquito repellent, water. Lunch provided by most tours.

activities.text: Paddle down the Macal River by canoe from San Ignacio, about three hours of leisurely paddling with swimming stops. Green iguanas, birds, herons. More lively and less touristy than organized tours. Full-day rentals from several providers on Burns Avenue, about 40 US dollars per person.

practical_info.tip: Avoid after heavy rains—the current becomes tricky.

visits.text: Cahal Pech is the oldest known Mayan site near San Ignacio, occupied from 1000 BC and abandoned around 800 AD. Perched on a hill ten minutes' walk from downtown San Ignacio, its plazas, ball courts, and royal burial chamber can be visited in two hours. Small museum at the entrance. Open from 6 a.m.

activities.text: Climb the temples of Cahal Pech—allowed, unlike other sites. Labyrinthine site buried in jungle, lightly visited, agoutis and iguanas on the structures. Combinable with Xunantunich the same day if you leave early. Entry 10 BZD, local guide available at the entrance for historical context.

practical_info.tip: Visit at opening for coolness and calm, before the groups.

visits.text: A hand-cranked ferry dating from 1954 takes you to Xunantunich. Free crossing of the Mopan River at San José Succotz, capacity four cars, running until 5 p.m. You get out of the vehicle during the crossing, only the driver stays inside. Then a one-mile climb up to the site entrance.

El Castillo reaches 40 meters, the second tallest structure in Belize after the Caracol temple. The pyramid is still climbable, side staircase to preserve the original steps. Stucco frieze on the east side, replica of the original, astronomical references to the Sun, Moon, and Venus. View all the way to Guatemala from the summit.

activities.text: Climb the side stairs of El Castillo—watch out in rain, the stones get slippery. Tomb of a royal dignitary, Lady Batzek, discovered recently, has upended perceptions of the role of Mayan women. Iguanas sunbathing on the structures, howler and spider monkeys in the surrounding canopy.

practical_info.tip: Entry 10 BZD dollars (5 USD), guides 30 USD for two people on-site.

visits.text: The Maya called Actun Tunichil Muknal the cave of the stone sepulcher. Used for ceremonies between 300 and 900 AD, it shelters over 1,400 artifacts left in situ and 14 skeletons including the Crystal Maiden, a young woman calcified by mineral drip. National Geographic ranked it the #1 sacred cave in the world. Accessible only with a licensed guide.

activities.text: Leave phone and camera at the hotel: strict ban since a tourist dropped their camera on a skull in 2012. Forty-five minutes walking in the jungle, three river crossings, swim to enter the cave, climbs on wet rocks. Socks mandatory in the sacrificial chamber. Count seven hours round trip.

practical_info.tip: Not for claustrophobes or non-swimmers. Book the day before with MayaWalk, Pacz Tours, or similar.

visits.text: The Garifuna of Hopkins descend from exiled Africans mixed with Arawak Island Carib people, deported by the British from Saint Vincent in 1797. The village of around 1,200 inhabitants remains a living Garifuna cultural center in Belize, with language, cuisine and drumming passed on as everyday life rather than as a show. Garifuna Settlement Day every 19 November.

Three miles of golden sand, wooden dugouts on the shore, palm-leaf bars, weathered dock, turquoise sea. No luxury towers, no cruise ship passengers, coconut trees, pelicans. Walk from one end of the single road to the other, laid-back vibe, welcoming locals. Wetlands to the north and south, bird watching.

activities.text: Spend an hour at the Lebeha Drumming Center at the north end of the village. Garifuna drumming lessons with Jabbar Lambey, founder since 1998, or simply watch the young locals playing in late afternoon. Free donation or purchase a CD to support the center. Drums made in Dangriga from mahogany wood and deer hide.

practical_info.tip: More lively on weekends, sessions almost daily in late afternoon.

activities.text: Hudut delivers: cassava fish, coconut milk, mashed plantain. Emblematic Garifuna dish, try it at Chef Rob's, Ella's Cool Spot, or Palmento Grove for the cooking class version. Also: cassava bread, conch ceviche, sere (coconut fish soup). Eat on the beach—that's the idea.

practical_info.tip: Book the cooking class at Palmento Grove the day before, about 75 USD per person.

activities.text: Rent a bike and ride along the beach to False Sittee Point south of the village. No hills, flat road, sea breeze. Deserted beaches on weekdays, swimming possible everywhere. Count 10 to 15 USD for the day from rental shops, basic bikes but perfectly adequate. Sunset over the Maya Mountains in the background from the dock.

practical_info.tip: Avoid the main road during downpours—it quickly turns into mud.

visits.text: On Caye Caulker, the local slogan “Go Slow” is painted everywhere and followed to the letter. No cars, golf carts and bikes, sandy streets, wooden bars on stilts, lazy iguanas on rooftops. The 8-km-long island separates the world's second-largest barrier reef from the mainland. Ideal for decompressing two days before the return flight.

The Split has cut the island in two since Hurricane Hattie in 1961. Now the main swimming and lounging spot: shallow waters, dock, Lazy Lizard bar with permanent rum punch and reggae. Go in late afternoon for sunset. North side of the split: calmer vibe, less party-oriented.

activities.text: Book the snorkeling trip to Hol Chan Marine Reserve, created in 1987, one of Belize's oldest marine reserves. Thirty minutes by boat, nurse sharks, stingrays, turtles, groupers, brain and star corals. Shark Ray Alley is the signature stop. Tours 75–100 USD per person, lunch included with the serious ones.

practical_info.tip: Full sun 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., bring reef-safe sunscreen—the other kind is banned.

activities.text: Avoid operators who feed sharks or let people touch wildlife. Caye Caulker Reef Friendly Tours, Salt Life Eco Tours, Black Lion Adventures: eco-conscious, small groups, clean motors. Ragga Sailing does the same thing by traditional catamaran, slower, more poetic. Seven-stop full day for enthusiasts.

practical_info.tip: Read reviews, explicitly ask "no feeding, no touching" before booking.

activities.text: A sunset on the dock beats any fancy hotel. Bars on stilts, Belikin beers for 5 BZD, fish tacos for 10 BZD, reggae music everywhere. Nightlife concentrates around Front Street south of The Split. Good street food spot: Fran's Grill stand, grilled grouper, plate 15 USD.

practical_info.tip: Bring cash—ATMs often break down and many places don't accept cards.

map_keywords: Belize City Philip Goldson International Airport

visits.text: Philip Goldson International Airport closes the loop, 30 minutes north of Belize City. The historic capital doesn't offer much to travelers and security is precarious: transit directly from the water taxi dock to the airport. Daily direct flights to Miami, Houston, Atlanta, plus regional connections to Guatemala and Honduras.

activities.text: From Caye Caulker, the water taxi drops you at the Belize City terminal, where a taxi takes you on to Philip Goldson airport north of the city. A faster option: the small plane run by Tropic Air or Maya Island Air, which links the Caye Caulker airstrip to the airport, flying over the barrier reef. If your flight leaves late and you have a few hours in town, the Museum of Belize, housed in the former colonial prison, traces the history of the country and its Maya cities. Get around by taxi rather than on foot.

seo.h1_title: Guatemala & Belize in 13 Days: Mayas and the Caribbean
seo.intro_paragraph: 13 days between Guatemala's highlands and Belize's Caribbean coast. Colonial Antigua, Lake Atitlán and Chichicastenango market, Tikal Mayan city, Cayo jungle and sacred Actun Tunichil Muknal cave, Garifuna village of Hopkins, snorkeling on the world's second-largest barrier reef from Caye Caulker.
seo.seo_hook: Antigua, Lake Atitlán, Tikal, ATM Cave, and snorkeling at Caye Caulker: 13 days between Mayan cities, Belize jungle, and Caribbean beaches—resort-style format.
featured_list: Antigua: UNESCO colonial capital, baroque ruins at the foot of three volcanoes
Lake Atitlán: 84,000-year-old caldera, Tz'utujil Mayan villages by lancha
Tikal: dual UNESCO site, Temple IV above the canopy
