itineraries.title: Guatemala and Belize in 15 Days: Mayan Cities and the Caribbean
itineraries.subtitle: From the colonial town of Antigua to the reefs of Ambergris Caye, fifteen days among volcanoes, Mayan temples and lagoon.
itineraries.notes: The Melchor de Mencos land border crossing requires two checks and a Belize exit tax payable in cash. Highland accommodation (Chancol, Cobán) is unheated: February nights there drop well below 10°C.
itineraries.climate: Best period: December to April, at the height of the dry season, which matches a February departure exactly. Expect 12 to 25°C on the highland plateaus (Antigua, Atitlán, Huehuetenango) and 26 to 29°C on Belize's Caribbean coast. Avoid June to October: daily rain in the Petén, deteriorated roads towards Semuc Champey and the risk of tropical storms.
specialties: Snorkeling sur la barrière de corail

visits.text: The Arco de Santa Catalina frames the Agua volcano along the axis of 5a Avenida. Painted yellow, it once linked the Santa Catalina convent to a neighbouring building so the nuns could cross the street unseen. Come before 8am: after that hour, tuk-tuks and groups block the view and the photo becomes impossible.

Canary yellow, laden with white stucco: the façade of the Iglesia de La Merced looks like no other church in Antigua. The adjoining cloister, ruined by the 18th-century earthquakes, is visited separately and houses a large central fountain. The church is free, the cloister is paid: start with the latter, the morning light is better there.

Capital of the Kingdom of Guatemala from 1543 to 1773, Antigua emptied out after the 1773 earthquakes, when power moved to present-day Guatemala City. The Palacio de los Capitanes Generales still lines an entire side of the Parque Central with its double row of arches. Sit near the fountain in the late afternoon: that is when the town comes out for a walk.

Ruined, the Iglesia de San Francisco el Grande remains one of Antigua's busiest sites: it holds the remains of Pedro de Bétancourt, a saint widely prayed to locally. A rebuilt nave on one side, open-air ruins on the other. The ex-votos hung near the tomb are worth the visit alone; allow half an hour.

activities.text: First night in a restored colonial house: the Mesón de María stands a stone's throw from the Arco de Santa Catalina. Its rooftop terrace opens onto views of the volcanoes and tiled roofs. Go up at sunset: on a clear day, Fuego regularly sends up a plume.

practical_info.tip: Listing and traveller reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g295366-d674090-Reviews-Hotel_Meson_de_Maria-Antigua_Sacatepequez_Department.html

activities.text: If you arrive before nightfall, head to the Mercado de Artesanías, west of the town. Textiles, jade, coffee from nearby fincas: listed prices are negotiable, but stay reasonable, as it is often the women producers themselves running the stalls. Closes around 6pm.

practical_info.tip: Bring quetzales in small denominations, very few stalls accept cards. Next stage: Antigua → Pacaya volcano, 45km, 1h20 by car.

visits.text: Dormant for nearly a century, the Pacaya volcano woke violently in 1965 and has barely stopped being active since. Its active crater bears the name of Alfredo MacKenney, a Guatemalan doctor who monitored its evolution for decades. The park is open from 7am to 6pm: leave Antigua early, as clouds often roll in after 11am and blot out the view.

activities.text: You will climb Pacaya with a local guide: this is the park's rule, and useful anyway for reading the landscape. Allow about 3 hours there and back over 5km, with modest elevation gain. Horses wait at the trailhead for those who would rather spare their legs, for an extra fee negotiated on site.

practical_info.tip: Pay the park entrance fee in quetzales on site; the guide is paid separately. Next stage: Pacaya volcano → Cerro Chino, 2km, 20 minutes on foot.

visits.text: Cerro Chino is the park's best viewpoint, and it is not the summit: this secondary cone overlooks the Meseta's black lava flows without requiring the full ascent. The contrast is stark between the pine forest below and the basalt field above. Closed shoes are compulsory, as the volcanic rock cuts thin soles.

activities.text: Guides call the smoking fissures 'los hornitos', the little ovens. Some visitors toast marshmallows there on a skewer, a gesture that has become an accepted ritual, and a pizza oven runs on the heat of the ground near the visitor post. Kitsch, but feeling the warm ground underfoot stays memorable.

practical_info.tip: Bring water: there is no supply point on the trail. Next stage: Cerro Chino → Antigua, 45km, 1h15 by car.

visits.text: Las Capuchinas is the most legible of Antigua's ruined convents, and the best explained. Its circular retreat tower, with cells arranged in a ring around a patio, resembles nothing else in Guatemala. The vaulted basement carries an echo: whisper there, children love it. Allow an hour.

The smell of damp stone and bougainvillea: the Convento de Santa Clara leaves its collapsed arches open to the sky. The nuns there were renowned for their bread, sold throughout the colonial town. It is the quietest spot in the centre at midday, when the better-known convents fill up.

The cacao and chocolate museum, two streets from the Parque Central, is free to visit. It follows the bean from pod to bar, with a tasting at the end. It is short, under an hour, and explains why Antigua has so many artisan chocolatiers within a three-street radius.

activities.text: If coffee interests you, several fincas around Antigua open their doors, with La Azotea and Filadelfia among the oldest. The tour covers picking, drying and roasting, tasting included. Book the day before: departures run at fixed times, usually in the morning.

practical_info.tip: Return transport from the centre is rarely included, check when booking.

activities.text: Free day, but Antigua is not quite a place to wander at random: the street grid, inherited from the 16th-century Renaissance plan, looks much the same from one block to the next. Spot the Agua volcano, always to the south, and you will not get lost. The cobbled streets are hard on ankles: trainers rather than sandals.

practical_info.tip: Many museums close between noon and 2pm: plan your lunch around that slot. Next stage: Antigua → San Juan Comalapa, 45 km, 1 h 15 by car.

map_keywords: Casa Museo Rafael Alvarez Ovalle Comalapa

visits.text: A cemetery wall as an art gallery: in San Juan Comalapa, the mural running along the Cementerio General tells the country's history, from pre-Columbian times to the armed conflict. The village's painters undertook it collectively from the 1990s onwards. Park below and walk up, as it reads in that direction.

Comalapa's painting tradition began in the 1930s with Andrés Curruchich (1891-1969), who took up oil painting to depict scenes of Kaqchikel life. His pupils carried the style on, hence the nickname "Florencia de América". The childhood home of Rafael Álvarez Ovalle, composer of the national anthem, can also be visited in the town.

activities.text: Painters' workshops often occupy the artists' own houses, around the square, and the door opens without ceremony. You buy directly from the creator, and the canvases are rolled up for transport. The village's craft market is more modest than Chichicastenango's, but considerably less crowded.

practical_info.tip: Always ask before photographing a person or a workshop. Next stage: San Juan Comalapa → Panajachel, 75 km, 1 h 50 by car.

visits.text: Stacked signs, marimba in the background, the smell of grilled corn: Calle Santander runs straight down towards the Panajachel jetty for several hundred metres of shops. It is noisy and entirely unapologetic about it. Walk down it in the late afternoon, when the light catches the volcanoes head-on at the end of the street.

Lake Atitlán occupies a caldera formed around 84,000 years ago and plunges to some 350 metres, making it the deepest in Central America. Three volcanoes close it off to the south: San Pedro, Tolimán and Atitlán, the latter at 3,537 m. Panajachel's archaeological museum displays pottery raised from Samabaj, a sunken Mayan city rediscovered by divers.

The Iglesia San Francisco de Panajachel looks unassuming next to the lake, and that is precisely what makes it interesting: a plain white façade, a bare interior, a legacy of Franciscan evangelisation. Ten minutes is enough. Then push on to the municipal market, two streets up, which is considerably livelier.

activities.text: A planted garden that cuts out the noise of Calle Santander: that is the best the Regis Hotel & Spa has to offer, with pools fed by volcanic hot springs reserved for guests. Book your evening slot as soon as you arrive, as they fill up fast.

practical_info.tip: Listing and reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g292008-d1210157-Reviews-Regis_Hotel_Spa-Panajachel_Lake_Atitlan_Solola_Department_Western_Highlands.html

activities.text: Boatmen call it the Xocomil, the wind that gets up in late morning and raises a short swell on the lake. That is why all serious crossings leave early. If you are prone to seasickness, schedule your lancha trips before 10am.

practical_info.tip: Public lanchas leave once they are full: there is no fixed timetable. Next stage: Panajachel → Santiago Atitlán, 20 km, 45 min by boat.

visits.text: Santiago Atitlán was the capital of the Tz'utujil kingdom before the Spanish conquest, and most inhabitants still speak Tz'utujil among themselves. The colonial church, on the square, dates back to the 16th century and retains period altarpieces and statues. A plaque there recalls the murder of the American priest Stanley Rother in 1981, during the armed conflict.

Here he is not called Maximón but Rilaj Mam, "the Great Grandfather". This dressed wooden figure, wearing a hat and smoking a cigar, moves house each year according to the ritual calendar: the boatmen and guides at the jetty know where to find him. A modest offering is expected, a second one if you take photographs.

Stacks of textiles, medicinal herbs, live poultry: Santiago Atitlán's market operates first and foremost for people from the neighbouring villages. Huipiles embroidered on a backstrap loom, with their bird motifs, are distinctive to Tz'utujil women. Tuesdays and Fridays are the busiest days; the rest of the week, things quieten down.

activities.text: You will cross the lake by private boat from Panajachel, around forty minutes depending on the state of the water. The crossing gives the best angle on the three volcanoes, better than any viewpoint on land. Sit at the front on the way out, at the back on the way back when the Xocomil picks up.

practical_info.tip: Bring a windbreaker: even in bright sunshine, the speed and spray cool things down quickly. Next stage: Santiago Atitlán → San Juan La Laguna, 12 km, 30 min by boat.

map_keywords: Calle de las Sombrillas San Juan La Laguna
Galerias de arte San Juan La Laguna

visits.text: Calle de las Sombrillas climbs from the San Juan La Laguna jetty towards the centre, beneath a ceiling of colourful umbrellas. The façades on both sides are painted by village artists on Mayan themes. It is short, a five-minute walk, but it is the backbone of the town: everything starts from there.

San Juan's painting galleries are worth more than their reputation as tourist shops suggests. The local naive style depicts daily life and Mayan legends, often seen from above, as if the painter were perched overhead. Sellers roll up the canvases for transport, which solves the luggage question.

activities.text: You will visit one of the Tz'utujil weavers' cooperatives, where the cotton is dyed using only plants: indigo, avocado bark, cochineal. The backstrap loom demonstration lasts around twenty minutes and needs no appointment. Some cooperatives also offer workshops lasting several hours, to be booked the day before.

practical_info.tip: Prices are fixed at the cooperatives: do not haggle, as the profit goes to the weavers.

activities.text: A village café worth the detour: the La Voz cooperative brings together producer families from the surrounding plots and gives tours of its plantations. The tour covers varieties, altitude and processing, then finishes with a cup. The café next door, on the main street, serves the same beans if time is short.

practical_info.tip: The finca tour is booked directly at the La Voz café, down the street. Next stage: San Juan La Laguna → Panajachel, 15 km, 40 min by boat.

visits.text: If you return from San Juan La Laguna before 4pm, the Reserva Natural Atitlán, on the northern edge of Panajachel, offers one last breath of fresh air: suspension trails, a waterfall, a butterfly enclosure and spider monkeys in semi-liberty. Allow an hour and a half of easy walking. The entrance closes in the mid-afternoon, so check the time before setting off.

activities.text: End of the day on the Panajachel jetty: the lanchas come back in one by one, the volcanoes turn violet and the lake suddenly flattens out as the Xocomil wind dies down. It is the best moment on the north shore, and the shortest. A bench, twenty minutes, nothing else to do.

practical_info.tip: Dusk is brief at this latitude: be on the jetty by around 5.45pm. Next stage: Panajachel → Chichicastenango, 40 km, 1 h 15 by car.

visits.text: The Chichicastenango market spills out of the covered hall and takes over the streets, the squares and even the steps of the Santo Tomás church. Embroidered huipiles, dance masks, pottery, incense: it sells as much to villagers as to travellers. It is only held on Thursdays and Sundays, and your stage falls on a Thursday.

Clouds of copal on the steps of the Iglesia Santo Tomás: eighteen steps that worshippers climb while burning incense before going in. Inside, Catholic prayers and Maya rites coexist in front of the wooden altarpiece. Photographing the ceremonies is frowned upon: put the camera away on the steps.

It was in the archives of the Santo Tomás parish that a priest uncovered, in the eighteenth century, the manuscript of the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K'iche'. Facing the church, on the other side of the square, the small Capilla del Calvario receives the same offerings in noticeably greater calm. Five minutes' walk across, and the noise drops away.

The Chichicastenango cemetery is worth as much as the market, and almost no one goes up there. Graves painted turquoise, yellow and pink, incense burners lit between the rows: Maya rites are more visible here than at the church. Go up in the late morning, when the market is at its most crowded.

activities.text: Haggling is expected here, but within reasonable limits: start at around two-thirds of the asking price and stop there. Old textiles can be told apart from factory-made pieces by the evenness of the thread and the reverse side of the weave. Bring quetzales, cards are barely accepted between the stalls.

practical_info.tip: The market starts at dawn and empties out by around 3pm: arrive before 9am. Next stage: Chichicastenango → Chiantla, 140 km, 3 h 15 by car.

map_keywords: Parroquia Nuestra Senora de Candelaria Chiantla

visits.text: The Parroquia Nuestra Señora de Candelaria de Chiantla houses a sixteenth-century Virgin whose mantle is forged in silver, a gift from Spaniards enriched by the nearby silver mines in the seventeenth century. Hence its local nickname, the Virgen de Plata. The patronal feast on 2 February draws thousands of pilgrims; the rest of the year, the church is almost empty.

If the Cuchumatanes road is clear, the Mirador Juan Diéguez Olaverri, above Chiantla, opens out onto the whole plateau. The Huehuetenango-born poet has an engraved stele there. You climb quickly above 3,000 metres: the wind is bitterly cold even in bright sunshine, so keep a fleece in the car.

activities.text: Thin air, close-cropped grass, sheep among the rocks: the Cuchumatanes altiplano is like nowhere else in Guatemala. The road climbs in tight switchbacks from Chiantla and the landscape shifts within twenty minutes. Stop at the marked viewpoints rather than on the verge, as visibility is short on the bends.

practical_info.tip: Nights are very cold in February above 3,000 m: a hat and jumper are essential. Next stage: Chiantla → Huehuetenango, 8 km, 20 min by car.

visits.text: Restored in the 1940s, Zaculeu looks like no other Maya site in the country: pyramids with smoothed-over surfaces, almost like new. The approach is divisive, but it makes the layout of the plazas and ball court immediately easy to read. Capital of the Mam kingdom, the city fell in 1525 after a siege of several months, its defenders starved. The site is 3.7 km from the town centre.

activities.text: The Unicornio Azul is a remote finca in the aldea of Chancol, around 25km from Huehuetenango, a 1-hour-15-minute drive, and at nearly 3,000 metres of altitude. Eight rooms, dinner taken together, a fireplace. The generator switches off at night: a head torch is useful, and a hot water bottle is provided.

practical_info.tip: Listing and reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Feature-g1858021-d1850643-zft1-Posada_Rural_y_Ecuestre_Unicornio_Azul.html

activities.text: The horse ride at the Unicornio Azul is the real reason for this stage, more than Huehuetenango itself. About a dozen horses, open trails across the plateau, and an hour included in the room rate for two people. Let them know when booking if you have never ridden before.

practical_info.tip: The rooms are not heated: February nights are bitterly cold at this altitude. Next stage: Huehuetenango → Sacapulas, 100 km, 2 h 45 by car.

visits.text: Sacapulas sits in an arid canyon at just 1,200 metres, even though the road descends to it from passes above 3,000. The climatic contrast is stark after just an hour's descent. The bridge over the Río Negro and the small-scale salt pans on its banks are the only two things worth seeing: it is a technical stop, not a cultural stage.

activities.text: Break the Huehuetenango-Cobán route here, rather than facing seven to eight hours of mountain driving in one go. The comedores in the town serve a decent lunch around the square, and it is the last reliable place to stock up before Uspantán. Fill up with fuel, as petrol stations become scarce afterwards.

practical_info.tip: Huehuetenango → Sacapulas: around 100 km, 2 h 30 to 3 h of mountain driving. Next stage: Sacapulas → Cobán, 200 km, 5 h by car.

map_keywords: Catedral Santo Domingo de Guzman Coban

visits.text: The Catedral de Santo Domingo de Guzmán has stood on Cobán's Parque Central since the mid-sixteenth century, when the Dominicans founded the town. Charles V had named it the 'Ciudad Imperial'. There is a display case of old silverwork to the right of the altar. Fifteen minutes is enough, and the square outside remains the best point of reference.

Beneath tree ferns several metres tall, the Vivero Verapaz lines up thousands of orchids, including a wide range of miniature varieties - a magnifying glass is provided. You arrive in peak season: flowering culminates between October and February. The Monja Blanca, the national flower, is of course a must-see.

Cobán's architecture is explained by German immigration that began in the 1860s, which made coffee and cardamom the driving forces of Alta Verapaz. The steep-roofed houses of the centre still bear the trace of it. The town is perched in cloud forest: it drizzles intermittently even in the dry season.

activities.text: The Coffee Tour at the Chicoj finca, a community-run cooperative, takes place around twenty minutes from Cobán. The tour follows the whole chain, from cherry to roasted bean, and ends with a tasting. A zipline circuit crosses the plantations for those who want something other than a walking visit.

practical_info.tip: Book the day before: guided tours leave at fixed times.

activities.text: If you arrive before nightfall, the Casa Gaia occupies a private reserve with garden and trails, about twenty minutes' walk from the centre. The restaurant serves dinner on request, which saves going back down into town. February is cool in Cobán: bring something warm for the evening.

practical_info.tip: Listing and reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g612400-d2062858-Reviews-Casa_Gaia-Coban_Alta_Verapaz_Department.html Next leg: Cobán → Semuc Champey, 60 km, 2 h 30 by car.

visits.text: Semuc Champey comes down to a single geological anomaly: the Río Cahabón disappears beneath a natural limestone bridge 300 metres long, and above it tiered turquoise pools are fed by springs. The Q'eqchi' name means 'where the river hides under the stone'. A natural monument since 2005; entry around 50 quetzales.

The mirador is the only spot from which Semuc Champey makes sense, and it has to be earned: 45 minutes of steep climbing through the jungle, steps and roots. Do it first, before the heat and before swimming. Coming back down drenched in sweat, the pools take on their full meaning.

activities.text: You'll swim in the tiered pools, the deepest of which reaches about three metres. The travertine is slippery underwater: walk rather than jump and watch for the ledges between pools. Arrive before 10am or after 2.30pm to avoid the crowds and enjoy low-angled light.

practical_info.tip: The site opens around 8am and closes around 5pm; entry in quetzales, cash only.

activities.text: A rustic but perfectly guided adventure: the K'an Ba cave is explored candle in hand, waist-deep in water in places. Narrow passages, small waterfalls, slippery rocks. Tubing on the Cahabón is available right next door. Neither is included in your quote: pay on site.

practical_info.tip: Leave your phone and papers in the locker or a waterproof bag: the cave is done in water. Next leg: Semuc Champey → Sayaxché, 200 km, 5 h 20 by car.

visits.text: Sayaxché is crossed by ferry: no bridge spans the Río La Pasión here, vehicles board a cable barge. The town serves as a base for around ten Mayan sites in the area, Ceibal and Aguateca chief among them. Expect a wait at the ferry in mid-morning, when lorries pile up.

activities.text: The last real supply point before the Cráter Azul: petrol, ice, water and provisions are found here, not beyond. Lancha operators also have offices in town, which remains the best place to lock in the boat price before reaching the jetty.

practical_info.tip: Semuc Champey → Sayaxché: around 200 km, 5 to 5.5 hours, including a stretch of dirt track. Next leg: Sayaxché → Arroyo Pucté, 75 km, 1 h 45 by car.

map_keywords: Refugio de Vida Silvestre El Pucte

visits.text: The Arroyo Pucté jetty is the only practical access point to the Cráter Azul, a few kilometres down a dirt track past Los Josefinos. Free parking, a couple of ice-cream sellers, nothing else. It's also the starting point for the other springs of the El Pucté reserve, less visited than the crater itself.

activities.text: You'll only reach the site by lancha, from the Arroyo Pucté jetty or from Sayaxché depending on the route chosen. The crossing passes through river channels and flooded forest, with turtles and waterbirds along the way. Book the boat in advance: on site, prices harden noticeably.

practical_info.tip: Bring water, a hat and a picnic: there are no facilities on site. Next leg: Arroyo Pucté → Cráter Azul, 1 km, 15 min by boat.

visits.text: Water so clear navy blue that you can see the bottom several metres down: the Cráter Azul is a spring of the Río La Pasión, within the El Pucté wildlife refuge. Water lilies, submerged trunks and ochre and green vegetation form a kind of garden beneath the surface. Five to seven metres at the centre, almost nothing at the edges.

activities.text: Mask and snorkel change everything here, far more than swimming alone. The visibility lets you follow shoals of fish above the submerged vegetation. Watch out for the current if you move away from the entry point: it pushes harder than it appears on the way back.

practical_info.tip: Don't use sunscreen or insect repellent before swimming, the water is protected. Next leg: Cráter Azul → Flores, 100 km, 2 h 30 by car.

map_keywords: Iglesia Nuestra Senora de los Remedios Flores

visits.text: The island of Flores was Nojpetén, capital of the Itza kingdom and the last independent Mayan state: it fell on 13 March 1697, more than 170 years after the highland kingdoms. The Spanish built the church and the square on the site of the pyramids. The current name dates only from 1831.

The island is easily walked around in under an hour along the malecón, the promenade that runs along the shore of Lake Petén Itzá. Painted façades, restaurants on stilts, jetties: it is flat, shaded in places, and you inevitably return to your starting point. The best time is just before sunset.

activities.text: If the lake level allows, a late-afternoon lancha trip circles the island and runs along the northern shore, on the Tayasal side. Allow an hour. Prices are negotiated directly on the dock and split if you share the boat.

practical_info.tip: The level of Lake Petén Itzá varies considerably: some jetties are submerged for part of the year.

activities.text: The Hotel Villa del Lago occupies an easy-to-understand position: on the island, a few dozen metres from the cathedral and the jetty. Tiered terraces with lake views, breakfast served up high. Ask for a lake-facing room, the difference is noticeable.

practical_info.tip: Listing and reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g562625-d616836-Reviews-Hotel_Villa_Del_Lago-Flores_Peten_Department.html Next leg: Flores → Tikal, 65 km, 1 h 15 by car.

visits.text: The Gran Plaza at Tikal places Temple I, known as the Temple of the Great Jaguar, face to face with Temple II, known as the Temple of the Masks, flanked by the North and Central Acropolises. The first rises to 47 metres and served as the tomb of King Jasaw Chan K'awiil I. It can no longer be climbed; the second can, up to a platform halfway up.

Temple IV is the highlight of Tikal, and not only for its height, some sixty metres, one of the largest pre-Columbian structures still standing. A wooden staircase climbs to the summit platform, from where the other temples pierce the canopy. Go up early: the morning mist over the jungle is worth the wake-up call.

Tikal was occupied from the 6th century BCE to the 10th century, and the park, created in 1955, was the country's first protected area; UNESCO listed it in 1979 as a mixed site, both cultural and natural. The North Acropolis covers tombs dating back to 400 BCE. Allow 4 to 6 hours to cover the marked trails.

If the heat leaves you with energy in the afternoon, the Mundo Perdido, west of the Gran Plaza, is markedly quieter. Its great pyramid is among the oldest structures on the site. The paths there stay shaded throughout, which makes all the difference past midday.

activities.text: You will hear the howler monkeys well before you see them: their roar carries several hundred metres and never fails to startle. Toucans, coatis and ocellated turkeys cross paths on the trails. Walk slowly and look up near Temple IV, that is where most birds are seen.

practical_info.tip: The park opens at 6am and closes at 6pm; the sunrise and sunset slots carry an extra charge.

activities.text: A vast site but poorly signposted for those travelling alone: an English-speaking guide genuinely transforms a visit to Tikal, linking stelae, raised causeways and dynasties. It is included in your programme. Bring 2 litres of water per person, the humidity of the Petén wears you out faster than the displayed temperature suggests.

practical_info.tip: Insect repellent is essential: mosquitoes remain active under the canopy even in the dry season. Next leg: Tikal → Melchor de Mencos, 65 km, 1 h 30 by car.

map_keywords: Puente de la Amistad Melchor de Mencos

visits.text: Melchor de Mencos is the only major road crossing between Guatemala and Belize, set on the Mopán River opposite Benque Viejo del Carmen. The bridge is called Puente de la Amistad, the Bridge of Friendship, despite a territorial dispute never quite fully resolved between the two countries. The crossing operates from 6am to 10pm.

activities.text: Two successive checks await you, Guatemalan exit then Belizean entry, passport in hand for each. Allow twenty minutes to an hour depending on how busy it is. Ignore the informal money changers who approach vehicles: the rate is poor and the service unnecessary, cards are accepted everywhere in Belize.

practical_info.tip: A Belize exit tax of around US$20 per person is paid in cash on departure. Next leg: Melchor de Mencos → Cahal Pech, 15 km, 30 min by car.

map_keywords: Cahal Pech Archaeological Reserve San Ignacio
Cahal Pech ball court San Ignacio

visits.text: Cahal Pech was occupied as early as 1200 to 1000 BCE, making it one of the oldest Mayan sites in western Belize. The name means 'place of the ticks' in Yucatec Maya, a reminder of the days when the hill served as pasture. Around thirty structures cluster around a central acropolis.

Small, compact, and that is precisely its appeal: Cahal Pech can be toured in an hour and a half without ever meeting the crowds of Tikal. You can still climb the structures here, which is no longer the case everywhere. Two ball courts and a royal burial chamber round out the picture.

From the top of the Cahal Pech acropolis, the Belize Valley opens out to the north-east and the Maya Mountains close the horizon to the south. The hill overlooks the confluence of the Macal and Mopán rivers: it was this control of the river that explains the site's location. Toucans are frequently seen in the trees in the late afternoon.

activities.text: The visitor centre is worth a look before the ruins: a model of the site, reconstruction paintings and an interpretive film. Fifteen minutes well spent, without which the structures all start to look alike. An English-speaking guide is included in your programme.

practical_info.tip: Site open from 6.30am to 5pm; admission is paid in Belize or US dollars. Next leg: Cahal Pech → San Ignacio, 2 km, 10 min by car.

visits.text: A border town with no monuments, San Ignacio is nonetheless the place where you come to understand Belize: Creole, Maya, Mennonite, Chinese and Lebanese communities cross paths along three streets. The Saturday morning market, on the banks of the Macal, brings all of them together at once. The rest of the week, the atmosphere is that of a quiet small town.

The Macal flows at the foot of San Ignacio, brown and wide, crossed by the Hawkesworth Bridge, a single-lane suspension bridge. Canoes and kingfishers share the riverbank. It is the best place to take the pulse of the Cayo District in the late afternoon, once the heat has eased.

activities.text: Perched on the hill just above the archaeological site, the Cahal Pech Village Resort puts the ruins five minutes' walk away. Thatched-roof cabañas scattered through the garden, two pools, views over the valley and the town lights. The climb up from the centre is steep: take a taxi with your luggage.

practical_info.tip: Listing and reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g291971-d561798-Reviews-Cahal_Pech_Village_Resort-San_Ignacio_Cayo.html Next leg: San Ignacio → Belize City, 130 km, 2 h 15 by car.

visits.text: The Belize Marine Terminal, on North Front Street, is where water taxi departures to the cayes are concentrated. It's a charmless shed, but all traffic to Ambergris Caye and Caye Caulker leaves from here, with several daily crossings. Check large luggage in at the counter, not on board.

activities.text: You'll board the water taxi to San Pedro: around 90 minutes, with a stop at Caye Caulker roughly halfway through. The boats are covered but fast, and there is some rolling. Sit towards the back if you're prone to seasickness, and keep a windbreaker within reach.

practical_info.tip: Arrive 45 minutes before departure: luggage check-in closes early. Next leg: Belize City → San Pedro, 58 km, 1 h 30 by ferry.

map_keywords: Front Street San Pedro Ambergris Caye

visits.text: Sand in the streets, golf cart engines, the smell of grilled fish: San Pedro is built along three parallel streets, Front, Middle and Back Street. Ambergris Caye stretches for dozens of kilometres, but all the life is concentrated here. Traffic becomes heavy in the late afternoon: walk along the beach instead.

A fishing village turned seaside resort, Ambergris Caye has kept its wooden jetties and houses on stilts amid the resorts. The Maya used it as a trading post between what is now Mexico and Honduras. The contrast between the almost empty north of the island and San Pedro Town is striking.

activities.text: The Portofino Beach Resort occupies the north of the island, about six miles from San Pedro. That is the price of peace and quiet. Seventeen rooms and an on-site dive centre.

practical_info.tip: Listing and reviews: https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g291962-d308879-Reviews-Portofino_Beach_Resort_Belize-San_Pedro_Ambergris_Caye_Belize_Cayes.html

activities.text: If you want to get around on your own, the golf cart is the only hire vehicle that makes sense on Ambergris Caye. Allow a full day to make the rate worthwhile, and be aware that the track heading north is bumpy. Driving licence required.

practical_info.tip: The golf cart journey between the north of the island and San Pedro takes around 30 minutes. Next leg: San Pedro, same accommodation, no road journey.

map_keywords: Hol Chan Marine Reserve San Pedro

visits.text: Hol Chan is Belize's oldest marine reserve, established in July 1987. Its name means little channel in Maya: it refers to a natural break in the reef, about twenty metres wide and ten metres deep. Expanded in 2016, it now covers over 40,000 hectares split into eight zones, up from four originally.

Shark Ray Alley was added to the Hol Chan reserve in 1999. Nurse sharks and stingrays gather here because fishermen used to clean their catch there: the habit has stuck. Nurse sharks are harmless, but avoid touching them, as it is forbidden within the reserve.

activities.text: You'll set off snorkelling across both zones, usually on the same outing. Allow half a day. A reserve entrance fee is added to the cost of the outing, payable on the boat.

practical_info.tip: Mineral sunscreen only: chemical filters are banned on the reef.

activities.text: Kayaking is better here than you'd think: inside the reef, the water stays flat all day and paddling gives access to the seagrass beds where turtles and rays pass through. Go out in the morning, before the trade wind picks up. Hotels in the north usually lend out the equipment.

practical_info.tip: Stay inside the barrier reef: the current in the channel is strong at low tide. Next leg: San Pedro → Secret Beach, 11 km, 1 h by golf cart on a dirt track.

visits.text: Secret Beach is no longer a secret at all: bars, jetties and music along the west coast of Ambergris Caye, facing the lagoon. The water there stays shallow for dozens of metres and is wave-free, which remains unbeatable for an effortless day out. Go on a weekday and in the morning, and the place changes completely.

activities.text: Allow an hour by golf cart from San Pedro along the western track, and it's bumpy from start to finish. Many prefer the water taxi. On site, chairs and parasols can be hired from the bars, with sun loungers included in the price of a drink at some of them. Free parking if you arrive by road.

practical_info.tip: San Pedro → Secret Beach: 6 km as the crow flies but 11 km by track, 45 min to 1 h by golf cart. Next leg: Secret Beach → Mexico Rocks, 7 km, 40 min by boat.

visits.text: Mexico Rocks, in the north of the island, lines up round coral heads in two to four metres of clear water. The site was added to the Hol Chan reserve during an expansion: entrance fee applies.

activities.text: A half-day snorkelling outing from the hotels on the north coast, often combined with Tres Cocos. The site is less crowded than Hol Chan and the coral is in better condition. The current can pick up: stay with the guide and get back onto the boat via the rear ladder.

practical_info.tip: Portofino → Mexico Rocks: 10 to 15 min by boat from the hotel's beach, with no transfer to San Pedro. Next leg: Mexico Rocks → San Pedro, 9 km, 45 min by boat.

map_keywords: John Greif II Airport San Pedro

activities.text: Hammock, pool or massage under a beachside palapa: most hotels on the north coast offer something to round off your stay at the island's pace. None of this is included in your quote — request and pay on site. Book in the morning for a late-afternoon slot.

practical_info.tip: Bring Belizean or US dollars in cash: tips are given in cash.

activities.text: If your return flight leaves early the next day, note that the San Pedro-Belize City domestic flight lasts only around fifteen minutes and flies over the barrier reef. Checked baggage allowance is limited to 20 kg, plus one cabin item of 5 kg maximum. Weigh your bags the night before.

practical_info.tip: Belize departure tax of around US$20 per person, payable in cash at the airport.

seo.h1_title: Guatemala and Belize in 15 Days: Mayan Cities and the Caribbean
seo.intro_paragraph: This 15-day itinerary links the Guatemalan highlands to the Caribbean coast of Belize. Antigua and its volcanic plateau, Lake Atitlán and its Tz'utujil villages, the pools of Semuc Champey, then Tikal and Cahal Pech before the barrier reef of Ambergris Caye. Departure from Antigua, return via Belize City International Airport.
seo.seo_hook: Colonial Antigua, Lake Atitlán, Semuc Champey, Tikal and the Belize barrier reef: 15 days from Mayan Guatemala to the Caribbean.
featured_list: Antigua Guatemala: former colonial capital, listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1979
Lake Atitlán: caldera around 84,000 years old, 350 metres deep
Semuc Champey: 300-metre natural limestone bridge over the Río Cahabón
Tikal: national park since 1955, mixed UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979
Hol Chan: Belize's first marine reserve, created in 1987

highlights: Antigua Guatemala, colonial capital from 1543 to 1773, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979
Lake Atitlán, the deepest lake in Central America at around 350 metres deep
Semuc Champey and its 300-metre natural limestone bridge over the Río Cahabón
Tikal, occupied from the 6th century BCE to the 10th century, and its Temple IV rising above the canopy
The Belize Barrier Reef and the Hol Chan Marine Reserve, established in 1987

itineraries.title: Guatemala and Belize: 15 Days of Volcanoes, Jungle, and Reef
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: November to April, the dry season, with temperatures of 18-25°C in the highlands (Antigua, Atitlán) and 25-32°C in the jungle and on the coast. Avoid May-October: daily rain, oppressive heat in Petén (30-35°C + overwhelming humidity), and a risk of hurricanes from June to November on the Caribbean coast. Visibility around the volcanoes and diving conditions on the reef are best during the dry season.

map_keywords: Arco de Santa Catalina Antigua Guatemala

visits.text: The aroma of roasted coffee accompanies your first steps across Plaza Mayor in Antigua Guatemala. The city was founded in 1524 and built on a grid inspired by the Italian Renaissance, at an elevation of about 1,530 m. Keep this half-day free of reservations: after the flight, Arco de Santa Catalina is more than enough.

activities.text: Walk without a set route between Arco de Santa Catalina and Plaza Mayor as you settle into the rhythm of Antigua Guatemala. The city fits within a grid of cobblestone streets, so you can’t stay lost for long. Go to bed early; tomorrow will be busier.

practical_info.tip: Don’t schedule any visits at fixed times on your arrival day.

map_keywords: Convento de las Capuchinas Antigua Guatemala

visits.text: Consecrated in 1736, Convento de las Capuchinas in Antigua Guatemala would be just another convent if it weren’t for Torre del Retiro. This circular tower, with eighteen cells surrounding a central courtyard, has no equivalent elsewhere in the Americas; some describe it as the continent’s first apartment building. Come in midmorning, when the light falls into the courtyards.

Two sites are enough; three is already too many: in Antigua Guatemala, the Baroque ruins quickly start to look alike when you visit them one after another. Iglesia de La Merced, with its yellow facade covered in white stucco, is the one you’ll remember once you’re home. Afterward, sit in a courtyard instead of rushing to the next convent.

Plaza Mayor in Antigua Guatemala still serves the role it was given in the 16th century: the center of the grid, a meeting place, and a spot for fruit vendors. Nearby, Catedral de San José shows what the earthquake of 1773 left standing and what it brought down. Late afternoon is best, when the light grazes the facades.

activities.text: If you want to understand why Antigua Guatemala lies in ruins instead of being restored, climb Cerro de la Cruz early in the morning. The view frames the entire city, with Volcán de Agua directly behind it. Allow about 30 minutes for the climb from the north side of the city, and avoid making the trip alone late in the day.

practical_info.tip: Go up early and with someone else; walking the trail alone late in the day is not recommended.

activities.text: End the day without a reservation, on a terrace or in a courtyard in Antigua Guatemala—that’s intentional. This city rewards taking your time far more than seeing everything: its cobblestone streets, volcano views, and courtyards are as worthwhile as its monuments. Choose where to have dinner once you’re there instead of making an organized stop at a workshop.

practical_info.tip: Keep the end of the day free to allow for unexpected delays and fatigue.

map_keywords: Parque Nacional Volcán de Pacaya Guatemala

visits.text: Almost continuously active since 1961, Volcán Pacaya nevertheless doesn’t require a multiday trek. The Smithsonian describes it as a complex basaltic volcano located 30 km south of the capital, with nearly continuous Strombolian eruptions for decades. Check the park’s status that morning: access and permitted areas change depending on volcanic activity.

activities.text: You walk over ash and cooled lava as you climb Volcán Pacaya, making the day more physically demanding than long. It is Guatemala’s most frequently climbed volcano, with a local guide as required by park rules. Closed-toe shoes, water, and a windbreaker: it’s noticeably cooler at the top than in Antigua.

practical_info.tip: Wear closed-toe shoes, bring water, and check park conditions that morning.

activities.text: Deciding against the hike remains a perfectly reasonable option at Volcán Pacaya. Authorities regularly close sections, and the Smithsonian notes that activity has persisted since 1961, with lava flows and explosions ejecting volcanic bombs. Ask about current conditions at the park station before paying for an excursion.

practical_info.tip: Be willing to turn back if your guide or the rangers ask you to.

visits.text: No passable road connects Santa Cruz la Laguna to the rest of the lake: you arrive by lancha from Panajachel, a ride of about 25 minutes. The Kaqchikel village is divided into two parts, with accommodations along the waterfront and the residential center perched above. Expect a steep climb or a tuk-tuk ride to get from one to the other.

activities.text: Put down your bags and stay by the water on this first evening. Santa Cruz la Laguna is one of the few villages on Lake Atitlán without road access, which explains its tranquility compared with Panajachel. The water here is particularly smooth in the early morning: save kayaking for tomorrow.

practical_info.tip: Check the public lancha schedule as soon as you arrive at the dock.

visits.text: To the Tz'utujil, he is Rilaj Mam, grandfather, before he is Maximón. This wooden figure, cigar in his mouth, moves to a different house each year in Santiago Atitlán: one of the village’s religious brotherhoods takes its turn caring for him. The guides at the dock always know where he is; bring a small offering and let those who are praying pray.

activities.text: Crowded, noisy, and still not designed for you: Santiago Atitlán’s market serves the village first. The busiest days are Tuesday and especially Friday, when vendors from neighboring communities arrive before dawn with fruit, medicinal herbs, poultry, and textiles. Ask before photographing anyone.

practical_info.tip: Ask before taking photographs and politely decline shopping stops.

visits.text: San Juan La Laguna has more than forty murals painted by Tz'utujil artists from the village, often accompanied by a sign explaining their meaning. This is not a neighborhood repainted for photos: the murals tell the story of Maya cosmogony and local history. Start on Avenida 5ta, the most colorful street, then slowly make your way uphill.

activities.text: You climb stairs for about twenty minutes from San Juan La Laguna to reach the lookout overlooking the village. At the top, the view takes in San Pedro, Tolimán, and its small Cerro de Oro cone. There is an admission fee, and the climb will make you sweat: bring water, a hat, and shoes with good traction.

practical_info.tip: Wear shoes with good traction: the streets climb steeply from the dock.

activities.text: Founded in 1996, the Casa Flor Ixcaco cooperative grows its own cotton and makes its dyes from indigo, avocado, or cochineal, which makes all the difference compared with a souvenir shop. Each piece bears the name and photo of the woman who wove it. Watching the demonstration does not obligate you to buy anything.

practical_info.tip: The cooperatives charge no admission fee: you are under no obligation to buy anything.

visits.text: In the early morning, Lake Atitlán can be smooth enough to reflect the three volcanoes upside down. Its basin occupies a caldera formed about 84,000 years ago, and it is the deepest lake in Central America, at around 340 meters. Head out early: the wind often picks up during the morning.

activities.text: Weather permitting, you can walk along the northern shore between Santa Cruz la Laguna, Jaibalito, and Tzununá on a trail about 5 km long carved into the hillside. Allow 2 hours, with views of the Atitlán, Tolimán, and San Pedro volcanoes. Otherwise, go kayaking in the early morning, while the water is still smooth.

practical_info.tip: Walk in the morning: the wind and waves often pick up after noon.

visits.text: Copal incense burns on the eighteen steps of the Iglesia de Santo Tomás in Chichicastenango, built in 1540. It was in the adjoining convent that Francisco Ximénez transcribed the Popol Vuh in the early 18th century. The large market takes place on Thursdays and Sundays; on other days, the village is quiet.

activities.text: Start your visit to Chichicastenango’s market at the food stalls rather than the handicraft stalls: the atmosphere changes immediately. Vendors arrive at dawn, activity peaks in midmorning, and things wind down in the early afternoon. Keep your bag in front of you in the crowd.

practical_info.tip: Come early in the morning on a Thursday or Sunday, keeping your bag in front of you.

visits.text: The last independent Maya kingdom to fall, Nojpetén held out until March 10, 1697, nearly two centuries after the conquest of the highlands. The island is now called Flores, and stones from the destroyed temples were used to build the colonial town. The church plaza still occupies the highest point, on the exact site of the ancient temples.

activities.text: Keep this evening’s plans light. Chichicastenango’s market, 4 hours on the road, and a flight have already filled the day. Walking all the way around the island of Flores takes twenty minutes, and that is plenty for tonight. Drink considerably more water than usual: Petén is hot and humid.

practical_info.tip: Keep the evening light: it has already been a long day.

visits.text: The water at Cráter Azul is clear enough to see the garden of submerged plants from the lancha. This spring feeds the Río La Pasión near Sayaxché, with a depth of about five to seven meters at the center depending on the season. Bring a snorkeling mask, water shoes, and a towel: there are no lounge chairs or snack stands on site.

activities.text: You reach Cráter Azul by lancha from the Arroyo Pucté dock, after driving through Las Cruces and Los Josefinos. The boat ride takes about 45 minutes and is already part of the experience: howler monkeys along the banks, birds, and sometimes a caiman. A life jacket is provided; a dry bag is essential.

practical_info.tip: Bring a dry bag and use the life jacket if you get tired in fresh water.

activities.text: The best part is not always the crater itself. A five-minute walk away, a second lagoon with equally clear water draws far fewer visitors. Ask about it before leaving, as it is not always included. Do not use sunscreen or insect repellent in the water.

practical_info.tip: No sunscreen or insect repellent in the water: the site is a wildlife refuge.

map_keywords: Nuestra Señora de los Remedios Cathedral Flores

visits.text: Walk all the way around the island of Flores: twenty minutes is enough. The cobblestone streets climb gently toward the Catedral de Nuestra Señora de los Remedios, and Lake Petén Itzá is visible from almost everywhere. Save the western shore for late morning.

activities.text: If you want to fill the morning, a lancha ride on Lake Petén Itzá is the most relaxing option before heading into the jungle. Boats leave from the island’s docks. Otherwise, spend the morning having coffee on an outdoor terrace: tomorrow starts when Tikal park opens.

practical_info.tip: Have the agency quote a price for this option rather than paying on site.

visits.text: You hear the calls of howler monkeys long before you reach the temples when you arrive at Tikal National Park early in the morning. The park protects 57,600 hectares of forest, marshes, and savanna, with five species of wild cats, including the jaguar, and more than 300 bird species. Staying inside the park lets you enter at opening time, before the buses from Flores arrive.

Tikal’s Gran Plaza brings together the main sights: two temples facing each other, an acropolis, and a lawn surrounded by jungle. The central monumental area covers only about 400 hectares, within a site of which just 15% has been cleared. Choose two or three complexes and let go of trying to see everything.

activities.text: Hire a French-speaking guide for the first half of the visit, then walk between the complexes on your own. Tikal National Park is one of UNESCO’s few mixed World Heritage sites, listed for both its archaeology and its biodiversity: a guide is as useful for spotting spider monkeys as for interpreting the stelae. Bring water, insect repellent, and closed-toe shoes.

practical_info.tip: Enter at opening time: temperatures rise very quickly after 10 a.m.

activities.text: If you quickly tire of archaeological sites, look at the forest instead of the stones. The park lies within the Maya Biosphere Reserve, which spans more than two million hectares. The trails between the temple complexes are flat and shaded: this is often where the best moments of the day happen.

practical_info.tip: The shaded trails between the temples are more pleasant than the open plazas.

visits.text: Yaxhá occupies the northern shore of the lagoon of the same name and remains Guatemala’s third-largest Maya site, after Tikal and El Mirador. Templo 216, known as the Temple of the Red Hands, is reached by a wooden staircase and overlooks the jungle and the two lakes. The site is on the road to Melchor de Mencos: stop around midday.

activities.text: Smaller than Tikal but far less visited, Yaxhá can often be explored almost alone, among nine plazas and nearly 500 structures. Howler monkeys, spider monkeys, and toucans are common here. Swimming is prohibited in the lagoon, which is home to a large crocodile population.

practical_info.tip: The last ten kilometers are on an unpaved road: a suitable vehicle is required.

visits.text: Built in 1949, Hawkesworth Bridge is a suspension bridge in San Ignacio. The town, which locals call El Cayo, grew up at the confluence of the Macal and Mopan rivers, about fifteen kilometers from the Guatemalan border. Settle in for three nights.

Burns Avenue is the hub of life in San Ignacio: restaurants, agencies, bars, and a constant stream of travelers between Flores and the coast. The Saturday market, beside the Macal River, draws producers from across the Cayo District. Walk there in the late afternoon; it is the only thing to do today.

activities.text: Book ATM Cave and Mountain Pine Ridge on the evening you arrive in San Ignacio: spots for the cave are limited, and there are few licensed operators. Staying at one place for three nights saves you two transfers and two rounds of packing and unpacking. Go to bed early.

practical_info.tip: Book excursions from a single base to minimize transfers.

visits.text: An archaeological site you reach by swimming. Actun Tunichil Muknal is in the Tapir Mountain Nature Reserve, a 45-minute drive from San Ignacio followed by a 45-minute hike with three river crossings. Entry requires swimming about ten meters; a helmet and headlamp are provided. Skip it if underground spaces make you uncomfortable.

activities.text: Leave your camera at your lodging: cameras are prohibited in Actun Tunichil Muknal to protect the archaeological remains. Only guides with a specific license may enter, with a maximum of six visitors per group. Wear quick-drying, closed-toe shoes and be prepared to stay soaked for much of the day.

practical_info.tip: Closed-toe shoes are effectively required; no cameras are allowed.

activities.text: The Maya called this place Xibalba, the underworld, and guides in San Ignacio still use the word. In the main chamber of Actun Tunichil Muknal, pottery and bones remain in their original positions, including the calcified skeleton nicknamed the Crystal Maiden. Follow the route marked out by your guide to the nearest centimeter.

practical_info.tip: Stay strictly on the marked route: a single step to the side can damage archaeological remains.

map_keywords: Rio On Pools Mountain Pine Ridge
Big Rock Falls Mountain Pine Ridge

visits.text: Rio On Pools stretches across a series of granite slabs and freshwater pools in the heart of the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve. The Belize tourism board describes it as a swimming and picnic spot, with natural slides carved into the rock. Check the depth before jumping in: wet granite is unforgiving.

You hear the roar of Big Rock Falls before you see the waterfall, tucked into the vegetation of Mountain Pine Ridge. It drops about 45 meters into a deep pool where you can swim. Access is via a steep staircase that takes ten to fifteen minutes to descend: save some energy for the climb back up.

activities.text: Visit both sites on the same day from San Ignacio: they are in the same reserve, and one day is more than enough. Expect red dirt roads; a 4x4 is strongly recommended, and registration at the ranger station at the entrance is mandatory. There are almost no shops in the reserve.

practical_info.tip: There are no shops in the reserve: bring water, lunch, and snacks.

activities.text: If you still have time, Rio Frio Cave is on the same route: its entrance is the largest in Belize, and a river runs all the way through it. It is a short, easy visit, unlike the rest of the day. Watch your footing; the ground stays damp.

practical_info.tip: Never jump in without checking the depth and current; the rocks are slippery.

visits.text: The Split did not exist before Hurricane Hattie cut Caye Caulker in two in late October 1961. Today, the channel is the best place to swim on the island, with a seawall, docks, and the Lazy Lizard on the shore. Go during the day for swimming and on weekdays for peace and quiet.

activities.text: A day with no plans is worthwhile here. After the cave and waterfalls, walking to the Split or doing nothing at all is exactly what you need. The water taxi from Belize City takes 45 minutes to 1 hour. Save your energy for Hol Chan tomorrow morning.

practical_info.tip: Keep the day light: the real marine highlight comes the next day.

visits.text: Established on May 2, 1987, Hol Chan Marine Reserve is Belize’s first marine protected area, created following a local campaign led by biologist Janet Gibson. The name means “little channel” in Mayan: the reserve centers on a natural break in the reef, about twenty meters wide and ten meters deep. Head out in the morning, when it is easier to see into the water.

Shark Ray Alley occupies Zone D of Hol Chan, added to the reserve in 1999. The site owes its existence to fishermen who cleaned their catch here: nurse sharks and stingrays became accustomed to coming, and never stopped. The water is shallow, making them easy to observe.

activities.text: Choose an operator that prohibits touching wildlife and coral and does not feed the sharks. Trips from Caye Caulker almost always combine Hol Chan and Shark Ray Alley. Use reef-safe sunscreen and stay horizontal above the coral.

practical_info.tip: This trip must be included in the quote, rather than charged as an extra on arrival.

activities.text: If the sea is rough, the operator will postpone the trip or switch sites, and that’s a good sign. The channel through the reef at Hol Chan concentrates both currents and marine life, making it spectacular but demanding. Listen to the briefing and stay together behind the guide.

practical_info.tip: An early morning departure is recommended, and no touching the animals.

visits.text: Caye Caulker has no large beach, and it’s best to know that before you arrive. The island is a laid-back base for trips to the barrier reef, with the local motto, Go Slow, posted just about everywhere. You can walk everywhere; taxis cost 5 Belize dollars regardless of your destination.

activities.text: The last day on the island is the one you’ll regret the least. The Belize reef runs along the entire coast, and there’s no shortage of outings: scuba diving, fishing, kayaking, or a flight over the Blue Hole departing from Caye Caulker. Don’t book anything in advance; decide that morning based on the weather.

practical_info.tip: Decide that morning based on the weather rather than booking in advance.
